w: An Elizabethan baroque flourish above the Dnipro, built as royal pageantry rather than fortress. Today it serves as the official residence of the president of Ukraine, standing shoulder to shoulder with the neo-classical Verkhovna Rada next door - politics and pomp side by side on the riverbank bluff.
s: Baroque palace on the Dnipro, now the president's residence
_facts: Official residence of the president of Ukraine
Elizabethan baroque style
Sited on the right bank of the Dnipro River
Adjoins the neo-classical Verkhovna Rada building

w: Since 1051 monks have carved cells into the caves beneath this hilltop monastery, and the complex that grew above became one of Eastern Christianity's great centres. The whole Pecherskyi district takes its name from those caves. Come for the gilded domes; stay for the underground labyrinth of relics and candlelight.
s: Founded 1051, still the heart of Eastern Orthodoxy
_facts: Founded as a cave monastery in 1051
Historic lavra of Eastern Christianity
Gave its name to the Pecherskyi District

w: A stainless-steel titan raised by Soviet planners to loom over the Dnipro, sword and shield in hand as part of the WWII history museum below her feet. In 2023, with Russian tanks back on Ukrainian soil, the hammer-and-sickle on her shield was quietly swapped for the tryzub - history rewriting itself in steel, mid-war.
s: A Soviet giantess, rearmed with Ukraine's own coat of arms
_facts: Monumental Soviet-era statue in Kyiv
Part of the National Museum of the History of Ukraine in the Second World War
In 2023 the Soviet heraldry was removed from the shield and replaced with Ukraine's coat of arms due to the Russo-Ukrainian War

w: Founded in the Middle Ages by the Kyivan Rus ruler Sviatopolk II, then demolished almost entirely by Soviet authorities in the 1930s - cathedral included. What stands today is a post-independence rebuild, reopened in 1999 and now headquarters of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine.
s: Demolished by Stalin, rebuilt gold dome by gold dome
_facts: Originally built in the Middle Ages by Sviatopolk II Iziaslavych
Much of the monastery was demolished by Soviet authorities in the 1930s
Rebuilt after Ukrainian independence, cathedral reopened in 1999
Headquarters of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine since December 2018

w: Kyiv's grandest medieval gate, named in imitation of Constantinople's own Golden Gate, had all but vanished by the 20th century when Soviet restorers rebuilt it in 1982 - with no surviving images of the original to work from. Historians still argue over how accurate the result is.
s: An 11th-century gate rebuilt from guesswork in 1982
_facts: Main gate in the 11th-century fortifications of Kyiv
Likely named in imitation of the Golden Gate of Constantinople
Rebuilt completely in 1982 though no images of the original survive
Contains a branch of the National Reserve Sophia of Kyiv museum

w: Architect Wladyslaw Horodecki built this Art Nouveau pile as his own apartment in 1901, covering it in concrete elephants, rhinos and hunting trophies - he was an avid hunter. Ruin forced a sale; a Communist clinic later moved in. Restored, it now hosts presidential ceremonies across the street from real power.
s: Concrete crocodiles and rhinos guard a presidential porch
_facts: Art Nouveau building in the Lypky neighborhood
Built 1901-1902 by architect Wladyslaw Horodecki as his own apartment building
Decorated with sculpted exotic animals and hunting scenes
Used as a presidential residence for ceremonies since 2005

w: The story goes that the Apostle Andrew climbed this steep hill and prophesied that a great Christian city would rise here - centuries before its Baroque towers were designed by the Italian architect Rastrelli in the 1740s. Perched above the Dnipro and the old Podil quarter, the view alone earns the climb.
s: Where legend says an apostle foretold Kyiv's future
_facts: Built 1747-1754 to a design by Bartolomeo Rastrelli
Rare example of Ukrainian Baroque
Legend holds Andrew the Apostle prophesied Kyiv's future as a great Christian city from this hill

w: Kyiv's grand boulevard was dynamited by its own retreating Red Army in 1941 rather than surrendered intact - the City Duma, stock exchange and finest hotels all went up. What rose from the rubble after the war is pure Stalinist neo-classical theatre, still the spine of the city.
s: Blown up by its own retreating army, rebuilt in marble
_facts: Main street of Kyiv, 1.2 km long
Deliberately destroyed by retreating Red Army troops during World War II
Rebuilt in Stalinist neo-classical style after the war

w: Planted at a busy three-way junction near the botanical gardens, this cathedral has switched ecclesiastical allegiance more than once - mother church of the breakaway Kyiv Patriarchate until a 2018 council folded it into the new Orthodox Church of Ukraine. A landmark for navigation as much as devotion.
s: A cathedral that changed hands twice in one century
_facts: Major landmark at the intersection of Ivan Franko Street, Taras Shevchenko Boulevard and Botanical Square
Under the jurisdiction of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine since the December 2018 unification council
Previously the mother church of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church - Kyiv Patriarchate

w: Twenty-seven floors hold roughly 15 million items - the world's most complete collection of Slavic writing, plus the archives of Ukraine's presidents and its leading scientists. Founded in 1918, the whole library was hauled east to Ufa ahead of the German invasion, then rebuilt.
s: 15 million books deep, once evacuated ahead of the Nazis
_facts: Founded in 1918
Contains about 15 million items on 27 floors
Holds the world's most complete collection of Slavic writings
Evacuated to Ufa during the German invasion of the Soviet Union

n: National Museum of the History of Ukraine
w: A vast, slightly overstuffed vault of Ukrainian history - some 800,000 objects, from archaeological digs and weapons to coins, manuscripts and relics of the 20th-century independence movements. Only a fraction, around 22,000 pieces, ever makes it onto display at once.
s: 800,000 objects tracing Ukraine from antiquity to now
_facts: Holds about 800,000 items in its collection
Around 22,000 items on permanent display at a time
Collections include archaeology, numismatics, ethnography and weapons

w: A guelder-rose branch in one hand, the Berehynia figure has watched over Maidan Nezalezhnosti since 2001 - atop a 61-metre column faced in white Italian marble, raised a decade after independence to mark the moment. The square beneath her has since hosted two revolutions and a war; the column just keeps standing.
s: A 61-metre column crowning the square of two revolutions
_facts: Victory column on Independence Square commemorating Ukraine's 1991 independence
Built for the 10th anniversary of independence in 2001
61 metres tall, faced with white Italian marble
Figure represents Berehynia holding a guelder-rose branch
